Regarding the pagoda at the Gucheng Temple in Qingzhou: The pagoda at the Gucheng Temple in Qingzhou was built by the monk Sengfu. It is said that when he first arrived at the temple, he saw a stone pillar standing there. He asked the local people about it, and they replied, "This is the pillar erected by the former King of Yan. The monk then said, "If this is indeed the pillar of the former King of Yan, then why is it not inscribed with his name? The people answered, "Because the king’s name was too vulgar, it was not recorded. The monk then said, "If that is so, I shall now engrave my own name upon it. Having said this, he took a chisel and began to carve his name into the pillar. At that moment, the pillar suddenly vanished. The monk was startled and filled with trepidation. He then went to the temple’s main hall and prostrated himself before the Buddha image, saying, "I am a man of shallow virtue who has come from afar. I have heard that the Tathāgata possesses the power to know the minds of others. I have committed an offense; may the World-Honored One forgive me. After he had finished speaking, he looked up and saw the stone pillar reappear in its original position. Seeing this, the monk’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately began to construct the pagoda. When the foundation was laid, he dug down several feet and discovered a stone slab. Upon opening it, he found inside a small bronze vessel containing a single pearl. The monk took the pearl and offered it to the Buddha image. That night, he dreamed that the Buddha appeared to him and said, "This pearl is the relic of the Buddha Śākyamuni. Because you have offered it to the Buddha, you shall attain the fruit of Arhatship. Upon waking, the monk felt great joy and subsequently completed the construction of the pagoda. Later, when the pagoda was opened for veneration, the pearl was still present within it. Thus, it is known that the pagoda at the Gucheng Temple in Qingzhou was established through these auspicious conditions.

In the level ground of the rear garden at Jianye,
he obtained a golden image;
he then investigated its original circumstances.
It was constructed by King Aśoka at the beginning of the Zhou dynasty and enshrined in Jiangfu. How is this known?
Since the Qin, Han, and Wei dynasties, there had been no Buddhist Dharma;
how then could there have been images buried in the ground in the region south of the Yangtze?
When Sun Hao obtained them, he had no prior faith in such things.
He did not treat him with much respect,
instead placing him in the latrine to attend to the cleaning implements.
This continued until the eighth day of the fourth month.
Hao, while playing in the latrine, said,
"Today is the eighth day, the time for bathing the Buddha," and then urinated on the head of the statue.
Immediately thereafter, his body became swollen;
the private parts were especially severe,
causing him to cry out in agony.
The Grand Historian’s divination stated:
"This is caused by having offended a great deity.
Thereupon, offerings were made everywhere to the gods and spirits, yet in the end, no efficacy was achieved.
Among the courtesans was one who had long been a believer in the Buddha, who said,
"The Buddha is a great deity;
Your Majesty has just defiled him."
"He may now be invited.
Sun Hao believed him and,
prostrating himself upon his pillow, took refuge in the Buddha.
After a short while, he was healed.
Thereupon, a horse-drawn carriage was used to welcome the śramaṇa Senghui into the palace,
where the statue was bathed with fragrant water and the king offered his apologies.

Regarding the account of the stone image from Wujun floating down the Yangtze River during the Western Jin dynasty, as recorded by Sengyou in the *Chu sanzang jiji*: In the first year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min of the Western Jin (the third year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin), a stone image drifted down the river to the vicinity of Wujun. At that time, the local people were struck with awe and reverence; they constructed a boat to transport it ashore and erected a pavilion to house it. Subsequently, the image was moved to Jianchu Monastery. It is said that when the image was first brought to the monastery, it emitted a brilliant light that illuminated the entire hall. Furthermore, whenever the monks chanted the scriptures, the image would manifest various auspicious signs. This account is based on the records of the monk Daoxuan of the Kaiyuan era. It is also noted that the image was originally cast during the reign of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin. Later, during the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai, the image was transported to Wujun. During the reign of Emperor Min, it again floated down the river to the aforementioned location. Thus, the image has been enshrined at Jianchu Monastery for over one thousand years. Fishermen gathered at the mouth of the Hudu Estuary in Songjiang, Wu County, Wu Commandery.
From afar, they saw two figures appearing and floating upon the water in the sea;
the fishermen suspected them to be sea deities.
They summoned shamans and priests, prepared sacrificial animals and offerings, and set out to welcome him;
however, as the wind and waves grew ever more violent, they returned in terror and fear.
Furthermore, there were followers of the Five Pecks of Rice Way and the Yellow Emperor and Laozi who said:
"This is the Master of Heaven.
They went together again to receive him,
but the wind and waves were as they were before.
There was a lay follower of the Buddha named Zhu Ying of Huavillage in Wu County, who,
upon hearing this, sighed in admiration and said:
"Could this not be the descent of the Great Awakened One?
Thereupon, having purified themselves through fasting, he and several others—including the nun Bani of Dongyun Temple and other believers—went to the mouth of the river.
They prostrated themselves and invited him [in], whereupon the wind and waves were immediately stilled.
The two men floated down the river and followed the tide into the estuary;
as they drew closer, it gradually became clear that they were stone statues.
Just as he was about to receive it with his hands,
before his strength could be fully exerted,
he attempted to lift it up.
He rose up with a fluttering motion and immediately returned to Tongxuan Temple,
where he examined the inscription on the back of the statue.
The first was named Vipaśyin;
the second was named Kāśyapa.
Their imperial eras cannot be measured.
The traces of his departure were clearly manifest;
he rose to a height of seven feet and established the Dharma seat.
When he wished to install two statues,
although there were dozens of people, they were unable to move them at all.
He again made a formal request, and suddenly they could be raised.
This was reported to the throne,
and among the officials and commoners of the court, nine out of ten turned their hearts toward him.
Then, the śramaṇa Shi Fayuan arrived from the Western Regions.
The *Jingji* states that there are two stone statues in the east,
and it is said that those who make offerings to and pay homage at the Aśoka Stūpa will eliminate the sins accumulated over kalpas.
Furthermore, another tradition states that twelve Śramaṇas from India escorted the image to the commandery; however,
the image stood upon the water, neither sinking nor moving forward.
He submitted a report on these circumstances for imperial perusal.

An edict was issued permitting [the image] to remain in Wu Commandery; this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the *Record of Manifested Marvels* (*Jingyi ji*). Subsequently, the Princess Changyang of the capital heard of these auspicious traces.
Therefore, he dispatched a person to Tongxuan Temple to sketch it.
While the model was being prepared for carving at the capital, the manifestation of the image was about to be revealed.

It is said that during the Western Jin dynasty, at Mount Tai, there were auspicious circumstances regarding seven sets of golden images; specifically, the fourth of these concerns the temple of Master Lang at Jinyu Valley. During the Western Jin, at Mount Tai... [the temple of] Master Lang.
In the past, when the Central Plains were embroiled in turmoil and the Yongjia era lost its governance,
there was a śramaṇa named Shi Senglang,
whose secular surname was Li.
Ji Ren traveled west and returned east;
together with the two monks Zhan and Yi, he entered Mount Dong (Mount Tai).
He divined a northwestern cliff to be his place of final rest;
it was constantly shaded by clouds, and both the scholar-officials and the common folk regarded this with wonder.
His auspicious resonance shook distant lands, and he brought his studies to completion while dwelling in quiet seclusion.
At that time, the empire was without a sovereign and heroes were biding their time;
from Qin, Song, Yan, and Zhao, there were none who did not send letters expressing their profound reverence.
He allocated the taxes from the district to honor the Buddha;
thus, there are golden and copper statues sent by seven kingdoms—Koguryo, Huguk, Okuk, Wokuk, Kunlun, Beida, and another—along with a statue made of gold and copper.
Lang served him with the utmost propriety, constantly presenting auspicious omens.
Now they dwell together in a single hall whose doors and windows are always open, yet birds and sparrows dare not tread upon them;
all revere and marvel at this.
The temple has existed for approximately three hundred and fifty years until the present day;
its pagoda foundations and structural layout remain as they were originally.
During the Sui dynasty, it was renamed the Shentong Daochang (Divine Path Practice Site).
The temple was subsequently established there.
During the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin dynasty, a golden image emerged from the shallows at Zhuzhuan; this was in the fifth year of the fifth cycle (360 CE).
At that time, Gao Kui served as the Governor of Danyang.
Whenever he traveled to and from the imperial palace, he frequently observed extraordinary lights appearing at Zhanghou Bridge and the marshes.
He then dispatched an official to search for them, who recovered a golden image;
it was an ancient artifact from the Western Regions, both its halo and pedestal being incomplete.
Hui-li descended from the carriage and placed the image upon it.
When they reached the entrance of Changgan Lane,
the ox would no longer move forward.
Kui stopped the driver and let the ox follow its own way;
they then proceeded directly toward Changgan Temple.
He had him installed there, and the capital was filled with a great stir of people coming to view and prostrate before him;
those who attained awakening were exceedingly numerous.
It was said that at midnight, it would invariably emit a golden light for about a year.
During this time, a fisherman from Linhai County named Zhang Houshi saw a copper lotus pedestal floating upon the sea, radiating a crimson glow.
He then hurriedly dispatched a boat to retrieve him and escorted him up to the palace.
The Emperor ordered that An Kui’s feet be examined.
It coincided perfectly with this.
After some time, five monks from the Western Regions arrived at Huikai’s residence, shaking their mendicant staffs, and said,
"We have previously traveled to India."
He obtained an image of King Aśoka;
however, encountering chaos upon arriving at Ye, he concealed it by the riverbank.
Once the royal roads were reopened, he searched for it, but its location was lost.
A recent dream recounted that he had gone to Jiangdong and was captured by Gao Kui,
whereupon he was at Aśoka Monastery.
Therefore, he traveled from afar to seek refuge with me,
desiring to pay a single prostration.
Hui-k’lei led him to the temple.
When the five monks saw the image, they sighed deeply and wept; the image emitted light for their sake, illuminating the interior of the hall and circling the forms of the monks.
The monks said:
"The original halo is currently at a distance;
it too shall soon arrive.
Thereupon, the five monks remained there to make offerings.
In the first year of the Xi'an era, Dong Zongzhi,
a pearl diver from Hepu in Jiaozhou of Nanhai, frequently observed a light beneath the sea floating upon the water's surface. Upon searching for it,
he discovered the Buddha’s radiance.
This was reported to the Emperor.
Emperor Jianwen issued an imperial decree to bestow a statue [of the Buddha] upon him;
its hollows matched exactly and its luster was no different.
For more than forty years,
the auspicious light gradually illuminated the lotus pedestal until it was fully revealed.
On the flower pedestal of this image, there is writing in a Western region script.
Most of those who came did not recognize it;
only the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman said,
"This is an ancient Brahmin script."
This was commissioned by the fourth daughter of King Aśoka.
At that time, the ordinary official and śramaṇa Huìsuì wished to have it copied.
The temple master, fearing that the golden color might be damaged, said to Sui,
"If you can cause the Buddha to emit light and turn his body to face west, [I shall allow it]."
This was not within the reach of others.
Suì made a most sincere prayer and supplication;
in the middle of the night, he heard an extraordinary sound.
Upon opening the hall and beholding the image,
it emitted a great radiance;
[the Buddha] then turned his seat to face the west.
Thereupon, he granted permission for it to be modeled;
dozens of copies were transcribed and circulated wherever they went.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, seven heavenly beings and two bodhisattvas were added above the light.
In the second year of the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty,
Wang Lin stationed his troops at Jiangpu.
He was about to head toward Jinling.
Emperor Wu ordered him to travel upstream.
At the time the army set out, [the following occurred].
The statue’s body shook and it could not remain still;
he reported this to the Emperor, who investigated and found it to be true. Before long, the blades had not even crossed.
Senglin’s followers dispersed, and he fled north alone on horseback.
He subsequently ascended to the upper reaches of the river at Dading;
therefore, he expressed his feelings through this memorial.
During the Tianjia era, military uprisings broke out in the southeast.
The Emperor made a vow before the image,
and the rebels were driven back and subdued.
When he had finished speaking, light illuminated the halls and courtyards.
Before long, Dongyang, Min, and Yue were all pacified.
The śramaṇa Huixiao was the leader of Changgan Temple.
The reach of his transformative influence moved all things like the wind;
thus he constructed a multi-storied pavilion, causing its decorative paintings to exhaust the most extraordinary designs and its heights to allow for a boundless view.
At the beginning of the Era of Supreme Virtue, he further added the construction of the square pedestal.
From the Jin dynasty down to the Chen, throughout these five dynasties, there were no kings or ministers who did not pay him reverence.
During times of severe drought,
they would request that his image be brought into the palace.
He was conveyed in an imperial carriage,
which was further covered with a protective canopy.
While the monks were adjusting for the rain, it poured down heavily midway along the route.
It was always observed without fail.
During the Chen dynasty, when signs of misfortune appeared and rumors spread rapidly,
in the second year of the Zhengming era, the face of the image turned toward the west of its own accord.
Although he was indeed returning to his original state,
he reported the circumstances to the Emperor.
The Emperor invited him into the Taiji Hall to perform a vegetarian feast and ritual practices.
The image originally possessed a crown made of the seven precious gems,
adorned with pearls and jade,
weighing three jin.
At dawn, he placed the precious crown upon the image’s head; by the time morning arrived, the crown was hanging from the image’s hand,
while the brocade cap still remained upon its head.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor burned incense and made this prayer:
"If there is any ill omen in the state,
let this real crown fall off to manifest the sign of the calamity."
He continued to wear the crown upon his head;
when dawn arrived, it was found hanging as it had been before.
The sovereign and his ministers were struck with dismay.
When the Sui dynasty extinguished Chen,
the entire nation went into exile to the west with their heads bared and hands bound behind their backs,
just as had been prophesied.
When Emperor Gao of the Sui dynasty heard of this,
he issued an edict to send him to the capital for veneration within the Great Inner Palace,
where he personally attended upon him at all times.
An imperial edict was issued, stating:
"I am advanced in years and can no longer endure standing for long periods.
You shall have the Right Office (You Si) fashion a seated image according to my physical likeness."
He had an image made identical to the original and sent it to Daxingshan Temple.
When the image first arrived at the hall, its scale was so vast that it could not face the front of the building.
He then placed it facing north;
when morning came, it was positioned in the direct yang (the south).
Although the assembly marveled at this, he moved it back to face north.
When dawn arrived, he returned to the south as before.
The assembly all expressed regret and apologized for their previous negligence; they now diligently engage in copying his likeness.
I have compiled these accounts from various biographies.
I have compiled this record;
should there be anything not yet comprehensive,
it is my hope that readers will know it contains no embellishments.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Ningkang era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

In the final month of winter the following year, the preparations were completed and fully adorned.

That image emerged at night and traveled westward through ten thousand mountains,
leaving behind a single footprint whose imprint was carved into the rock.
Monastics and laypeople from the surrounding villages and towns flocked there all at once.
They greeted him with expressions of wonder and amazement, returning him to his quarters and making offerings to him as before.
